reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: Post-streptococcal autoimmune chorea and the commonest cause of acquired chorea in childhood, typically arising 1-6 months after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
One of the major Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever, and may occur in isolation (pure chorea) when other manifestations have resolved.
Peaks between ages 5 and 15 with a female preponderance; onset is often subacute over days to weeks.
Clinical triad of chorea, hypotonia and emotional lability; obsessive-compulsive symptoms and attention difficulties frequently accompany the movement disorder.

Classic bedside signs include the 'milkmaid grip' (rhythmic squeezing on sustained grasp), 'darting' or serpentine tongue on protrusion, and pronator (spooning) sign with wrist flexion on arm elevation.
Chorea may be markedly asymmetrical or strictly unilateral (hemichorea) in up to a fifth of cases.
Antineuronal antibodies cross-reacting with basal ganglia epitopes are implicated; anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titres may already be falling by the time chorea appears.
Secondary penicillin prophylaxis against recurrent streptococcal infection and rheumatic carditis is essential regardless of whether cardiac involvement is evident.
reference.pathophysiology: Sydenham chorea is an autoimmune disorder triggered by group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection in a genetically susceptible host. Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens (notably M protein and N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosamine) and neuronal epitopes generates cross-reactive antibodies that bind surface antigens on basal ganglia neurons, particularly within the caudate and putamen. Antibody binding activates calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II signalling and disturbs dopaminergic neurotransmission, producing dysfunction of the striatal indirect pathway and the disinhibited, involuntary movements characteristic of chorea. Neuroimaging and functional studies show reversible striatal inflammation and hypermetabolism, correlating with the usually self-limiting course as the immune response wanes.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome chorea
Chorea gravidarum and oral contraceptive-related chorea
Benign hereditary chorea and other genetic choreas
additionalInvestigations: Throat swab culture and anti-streptolysin O / anti-DNase B titres
Echocardiography to detect subclinical rheumatic valvulitis
Inflammatory markers (ESR, C-reactive protein) and full blood count
Autoantibody screen (antinuclear, antiphospholipid antibodies) to exclude lupus
Serum caeruloplasmin and copper studies to exclude Wilson disease
MRI brain (often normal or showing reversible striatal signal change)
Electrocardiogram for evidence of rheumatic carditis
redFlags: Signs of active carditis (new murmur, cardiac failure, pericardial rub) requiring urgent cardiology assessment
Severe generalised chorea causing dehydration, exhaustion or injury (chorea paralytica)
Fever, encephalopathy or focal deficits suggesting an alternative encephalitic process
Marked psychiatric disturbance or self-harm risk from emotional lability
Recurrence of chorea suggesting inadequate streptococcal prophylaxis
reference.prognosis: Most cases are self-limiting and resolve over weeks to months, though symptoms may persist up to two years and recur in a third of patients, particularly during pregnancy or with oestrogen exposure. Long-term outcome is dominated by the risk of rheumatic heart disease, making secondary antibiotic prophylaxis the key determinant of prognosis.
pitfalls: Attributing fidgetiness or emotional change to behavioural problems and missing an evolving chorea.
Excluding rheumatic fever because pharyngitis was not recalled or streptococcal titres have already normalised.
Omitting echocardiography because a murmur is not audible, thereby missing subclinical valvulitis.
Failing to institute or continue secondary penicillin prophylaxis, risking carditis with recurrent infection.
Over-sedating with dopamine antagonists when symptoms are mild and would settle spontaneously.
